Sarawud (Juy) Saleesongsom, PhD

Atmospheric Science and Environmental Geochemistry: advancing our understanding of air pollution through aerosol chemistry, acidity and thermodynamic modelling.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Environmental Science Research Center (ESRC), Faculty of Science, Chiang Mai University, Thailand

Hello, welcome :)

I am an environmental geochemist working at the interface of aqueous chemistry and atmospheric science. My research explores how acidic atmospheric aerosols are, how much water they contain, and how these properties influence chemical reactions within aerosol particles. I am particularly interested in iron redox chemistry, especially the oxidation of iron(II), which influences iron solubility and bioavailability and, ultimately, the supply of this essential micronutrient to the oceans.

Since July 2026, I have been a postdoctoral researcher at the Environmental Science Research Center (ESRC), Chiang Mai University, Thailand. My current research investigates the chemical processes associated with transboundary biomass-burning haze in Northern Thailand. I use thermodynamic models, including E-AIM, ISORROPIA and AIOMFAC, to estimate size-resolved aerosol pH and aerosol liquid water content (ALWC). My aim is to better understand aerosol acidity and water content during haze episodes and improve the representation of these properties in atmospheric aerosol models.

I completed my PhD in Environmental Geochemistry at Imperial College London in 2026, investigating how pH, temperature and chemical speciation jointly control Fe(II) oxidation kinetics in oxygenated aqueous solutions. As part of this work, I developed a temperature-dependent, nonlinear calibration method for glass pH electrodes that extends reliable pH measurements into the negative-pH range. I then applied this method to investigate Fe(II) oxidation under extremely acidic conditions.

My interest in environmental science began during my second year as an undergraduate at Imperial College London, when I took an Environmental Geochemistry laboratory course with Dominik. Learning how trace elements such as arsenic and iron influence environmental chemistry sparked my curiosity about the chemical processes that shape our environment. Since then, I have wanted to understand how chemistry can help us investigate and address pollution across rivers, oceans, soils and the atmosphere.

Today, my research brings together analytical chemistry, aqueous-phase chemistry, thermodynamic modelling and chemical kinetics to understand the chemical processes underlying atmospheric pollution.

I am always happy to connect with potential collaborators, students and anyone interested in my research. Please feel free to get in touch.

Highlights

Sarawud (Juy) Saleesongsom, PhDPostdoctoral Researcher · ESRC, Chiang Mai University

I recently had the opportunity to run a workshop on using Claude for data analysis and scientific visualisation with researchers at the Environmental Science Research Center (ESRC), Chiang Mai University.

With the recent release of Claude for Researchers, I’ve been exploring how AI tools can support researchers throughout the data-analysis workflow, from understanding and working with datasets to generating Python code and producing publication-ready scientific figures.

As part of our group’s work, I’ve been helping researchers use Claude to analyse our air pollution and PM datasets and turn the results into figures that are clearer, more reproducible, and closer to publication quality.

I’m particularly glad that I can combine my experience in coding, data analysis, and scientific figure preparation with these new AI tools. One of the things I enjoy most is sharing practical tips on how to improve figures and overall presentation.

This was Part 1, focusing on:
🔹 Introduction to Claude Cowork
🔹 Understanding the structure of Python code
🔹 Using Claude to work with scientific datasets
🔹 Generating and refining data visualisations
🔹 Tips for creating publication-ready figures

📊 If you’re interested in the presentation slides, feel free to drop me a message and I’d be happy to share them.

For those who may not be familiar with it, DPST (Development and Promotion of Science and Technology Talents Project) is a Thai scholarship programme supporting talented students in science and technology throughout their educational and research journeys.

I’m proud to be DPST Cohort 29. Last year, we celebrated 40 years of DPST, and it’s amazing to see the community continue to grow across generations of scholars.

A big thank you to all the senior scholars who shared their experiences, advice, and “inside information” on navigating academia and building a career in Thailand. It was incredibly valuable as we make the transition from our postgraduate studies into the next chapter of our careers.

And, of course, it was especially lovely to see my cohort friends again. Many of us have been on this journey together since high school, and it’s amazing to see where everyone is now, from DPST students back then to being a Dr. today. It feels like we’re entering another chapter of the journey together. ❤️

In the first photo, I had the opportunity to meet Prof. Dr. Yodchanan Wongsawat, a Thai academic who currently serves as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation.

Grateful for the people, the conversations, and the journey that brought us here. 🇹🇭

Research

My work combines laboratory experiments, thermodynamic and kinetic modelling, and field measurements of aerosol. It falls into four main threads.

Research highlights

What ties my research together is an interest in the Anthropocene: the idea that human activity has become the dominant force shaping the Earth. I want to understand how anthropogenic emissions change the chemistry of the air, rivers and oceans around us, and how that understanding can help us reduce pollution and its impacts. The picture below shows where my four research themes sit in that story; each theme page gathers the projects that belong to it.

Current and past projects

Aerosol acidity and liquid water during biomass-burning haze

Every dry season, agricultural and forest fires blanket Northern Thailand in haze. I measure size-resolved aerosol composition in Chiang Mai during haze and non-haze periods and use thermodynamic models to estimate particle pH and aerosol liquid water content. Because pH controls which reactions can proceed inside a particle, these estimates matter for secondary aerosol formation, metal solubility and health-relevant chemistry. A central goal is to test and improve how current thermodynamic models handle haze-period aerosol.

E-AIM · ISORROPIA · AIOMFAC · size-resolved sampling

Read more about this project →

Fe(II) oxidation kinetics across pH and temperature

The oxidation of ferrous iron by dissolved oxygen is one of the most pH-sensitive reactions in environmental chemistry, yet rate laws for very acidic, sulphate-rich conditions have been poorly constrained. My PhD produced a coupled pH–temperature logistic rate law for Fe(II) oxidation in sulphuric acid media spanning pH −1.5 to 8.0 and 5 to 65 °C, together with an experimental and computational framework for understanding how ligands and different acid systems alter the kinetics. The results feed into models of iron bioavailability in atmospheric aerosol and of sulphate-rich waters such as acid mine drainage.

UV–Vis colorimetry · PHREEQC · MINTEQ · HySS · DFT (Gaussian)

Read more about this project →

Measuring pH where the scale breaks down

Glass pH electrodes become nonlinear in concentrated acids and alkalis, which has limited quantitative work at negative pH. I developed a temperature-dependent nonlinear calibration, improved the statistical treatment of acid and alkaline errors over pH −4.5 to 15.5, and derived transferable correction factors so that other laboratories can apply the method without re-deriving it. This work includes open calibration software presented at Goldschmidt 2025.

ion-selective electrodes · Metrohm Titrando · Python · MATLAB

Read more about this project →

Adsorption kinetics of arsenic on metal oxides

As an undergraduate researcher (UROP) at Imperial College London I co-authored a study that revised the widely used pseudo-second-order (PSO) kinetic model for adsorption so that it explicitly accounts for changes in both adsorbate and adsorbent concentrations, rather than assuming a fixed excess of one over the other. To test the model, I extracted and meta-analysed 36 rate constants from 14 independent studies of arsenic adsorption onto Fe2O3 and TiO2, giving a quantitative picture of kinetic variability across systems. The work was published in Langmuir (ACS, 2021) and the dataset is openly available on Zenodo.

kinetic modelling · meta-analysis · Langmuir 2021 · Zenodo dataset

Read more about this project →

Earlier work: a global biogeochemical analysis of arsenic speciation in the oceans drawing on more than 10,000 observations (MSci thesis, Imperial College London; departmental Centenary Prize).
